title: PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agents via Machine-Checked Integrity Theorems and Scalable Community Trust
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agents via Machine-Checked Integrity Theorems and Scalable Community Trust
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Persistent memory is a largely undefended surface for injection and poisoning, and the same risk limits memory sharing among agents. We present PerMIT, a memory architecture with provable integrity guarantees under an explicit trust assumption: only user-typed inputs and values confirmed at a gate are trusted. PerMIT mediates the release and use of untrusted environment-derived values through a finite memory interface, while preserving agent-driven multi-turn planning and tool choice. Over this finite interface, we prove two integrity theorems that are also machine-checked in Lean 4, which together ensure that environment-derived memory reaches a sensitive action only if confirmed at the gate and influences the agent's behavior only through what the gate displays. Every attack in our threat model thereby reduces to a single auditable decision, which a human, an LLM verifier, or both can make in practice. On Trojan Hippo, PerMIT records zero observed attack success with self-verification and lightweight verifiers. Because each confirmation is a logged verdict on exact content, endorsements accumulate across users, and sufficiently endorsed items become community-confirmed with no further verification required. Under explicit assumptions, we prove and corroborate in simulation a co-scaling property: as the community grows, the risks of promoting poison and of wrongly evicting benign knowledge fall, while per-user verification effort does not rise. On $\tau^2$-bench, communities of up to 90 autonomous agents use PerMIT to build shared knowledge bases with no direct memory injection promoted, and the resulting knowledge significantly improves new agents on held-out tasks, suggesting a path toward agents that safely self-improve at test time.

report.summary: PerMIT secures LLM agent persistent memory with Lean 4 machine-checked integrity theorems, routing all untrusted environment data through a single auditable gate that scales into community trust.
report.background: Persistent memory has become the default way LLM agents carry context across sessions and tasks, but it is also one of the least defended surfaces in the stack. Unlike a single prompt, memory is written to over time and reused silently, so a poisoned entry from a web page, tool output, or another agent can influence dozens of later decisions. Existing defenses — input sanitization, provenance tags, retrieval filtering — are heuristic and offer no guarantee, and they degrade further when agents share memory, since one poisoned contribution can spread to an entire fleet. Meanwhile formal methods have matured in adjacent fields, and Lean 4 has become a practical target for machine-checked proofs. PerMIT sits at the intersection: it treats memory as a security boundary with an explicit trust assumption and provable properties, rather than a filtering problem to be tuned empirically.
key_points: PerMIT narrows trust to two sources: text the user actually typed, and values a human or LLM verifier explicitly confirms at a gate. Everything derived from the environment passes through a finite memory interface that mediates release and use, while still allowing multi-turn planning and tool choice. This turns a sprawling attack surface into one decision point.

The paper proves two integrity theorems and machine-checks them in Lean 4: environment-derived memory reaches a sensitive action only if confirmed at the gate, and it can shape agent behavior only through what the gate displays. Consequently every attack in the threat model collapses into a single auditable verdict rather than an open-ended filtering problem.

On the Trojan Hippo poisoning benchmark, PerMIT records zero observed attack success, including when the gate is an LLM self-verifier or a lightweight verifier rather than a human. Each confirmation is stored as a logged verdict on exact content, so the verification work is reusable rather than repeated per session.

Endorsements accumulate across users: once an item has enough logged confirmations it becomes community-confirmed and needs no further checking. The authors prove, and corroborate in simulation, a co-scaling property — as the community grows, the risk of promoting poison and the risk of wrongly evicting benign knowledge both fall, while per-user verification effort stays flat.

On τ²-bench, communities of up to 90 autonomous agents used PerMIT to build shared knowledge bases. No direct memory injection was promoted, and the resulting shared knowledge measurably improved new agents on held-out tasks — evidence for safe test-time self-improvement through collective memory.
report.impact: For the AI industry, PerMIT reframes agent memory as a formal-assurance problem, not a prompting trick. If the approach holds up, memory-layer vendors and agent platforms could face procurement questions about trust boundaries and auditable gates, much as databases faced provenance and access-control requirements. For developers, it supplies a concrete pattern: define an explicit trust assumption, funnel untrusted values through one mediated interface, log verdicts on exact content, and amortize verification across users instead of re-checking everything. For regular users, the payoff is agents that genuinely learn across sessions without silently absorbing malicious web content or tool output. The caveats matter: the proofs cover only the finite interface, not the whole stack, and safety still depends on gate reliability — human diligence or LLM verifier accuracy.
report.tools: Read the arXiv paper first, then the Lean 4 proof development to see exactly what the theorems assume. Try the Trojan Hippo memory-poisoning benchmark to reproduce attack-success numbers, and τ²-bench for multi-agent shared-memory evaluation. For practical integration, compare against existing memory layers such as Letta (MemGPT), Mem0, and Zep, and treat Lean 4 as the reference toolchain if you want machine-checked guarantees for your own agent protocols.
